questions.stem: The smallest potential difference named as a serious hazard is around:

options.explanation: One volt is harmless.
Twelve volts, as from a car battery, is not the quoted hazard level.
Even 50 V can pose a serious hazard to a person.
Mains voltage is dangerous, but the quoted hazard threshold is far lower.

questions.stem: Leaving a long cable tightly coiled while in use is dangerous because:

options.text: the trapped current overheats the wire
options.explanation: A coiled run cannot shed heat, so the cable overheats and the insulation can melt.
Static is not the mechanism here.
Insulation does not thicken in a coil.

options.text: the current doubles in a coil
options.explanation: The current is set by the appliance, not the coiling.

questions.stem: Moisture reaching live wires can:

options.explanation: Water does the opposite — it conducts.
Cooling is not the risk mechanism.
Nothing about moisture changes a fuse.

options.text: conduct electricity and start a fire or deliver a shock
options.explanation: Damp provides a conducting path for a short circuit or an electrocution.

questions.stem: The conducting core of a mains cable is usually:

options.explanation: Rubber is the insulating jacket, not the core.
Metals conduct, so they form the core.
Plastic is an insulator.
Glass is an insulator.

questions.stem: Which pair of materials both serve as cable insulation?

options.explanation: Both are insulators and both sheath wires.
Both are conductors.
Both are conductors.
Both are conductors.

questions.stem: Name the four safety features built into domestic appliances.
questions.modelAnswer: Double insulation, earthing, fuses and circuit breakers.

questions.stem: State two common electrical hazards in the home.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: damaged insulation exposing live wires, overheating cables, and damp conditions letting moisture conduct.

questions.stem: Explain why overheating cables can lead to electrocution as well as fire.
questions.modelAnswer: The heat can melt the insulation, exposing the live conductors inside, so a person who then touches the cable risks a shock on top of the fire danger.

questions.stem: A kettle's cable insulation is cracked near the plug. Name the hazard and the feature that should interrupt a resulting fault.
questions.modelAnswer: The hazard is damaged insulation exposing live conductors; the fuse in the plug (with the earthing of any metal parts) should melt or trip and cut the supply before a shock is delivered.

questions.stem: A plastic-cased drill with no exposed metal is:

options.explanation: It needs no earth connection.
The plastic case is itself a protection.
The fuse value is unrelated to the casing.
Insulated wires plus a non-metallic case are the two layers.

questions.stem: The two insulation layers of a double insulated appliance are:

options.explanation: Those are cut-off devices, not insulation layers.

options.text: the wire insulation and the non-metallic case
options.explanation: That pair forms the two layers.
Those are supply conductors.
Copper conducts — it is the core, not an insulator.

questions.stem: If a live wire touches an unearthed metal case, the case:

options.explanation: Metal cases do not melt at fault currents.
The case becomes live regardless of sign.

options.text: becomes electrified and shocks anyone touching it
options.explanation: The live contact makes the whole case a shock hazard.
Without an earth path the fault current stays small, so nothing trips.

questions.stem: The earth wire provides a path to earth that is:

options.explanation: A low-resistance path lets the fault surge flow freely.
High resistance would block the surge.
The fuse sits in the live wire.
The earth wire is bonded to the case.

questions.stem: After the fault surge reaches earth, the fuse:

options.explanation: Fuses never reset; breakers do.
Fuses store nothing.
The fuse limits nothing until it melts.
The surge through the live wire melts the fuse and isolates the appliance.

questions.stem: Why does a double insulated appliance not need an earth wire?
questions.modelAnswer: Its non-metallic case is itself the second insulating layer, so there is no exposed metal that could ever become live.

questions.stem: Describe what the earth wire does during a fault.
questions.modelAnswer: It carries a surge of fault current safely to earth while the enlarged live-wire current melts the fuse and cuts the supply.

questions.stem: Explain why the earth wire makes the fuse act during a fault.
questions.modelAnswer: The low-resistance earth path lets a very large current flow through live wire and fuse together, and that surge is what melts the fuse.

questions.stem: A washing machine with a metal case has its live wire chafe through onto the case. Explain the sequence that keeps the next user safe.
questions.modelAnswer: The case is earthed, so the fault current surges down the earth wire; the same surge through the live wire melts the fuse, and the machine is dead before anyone touches it.

questions.stem: A circuit breaker trips by means of:

options.explanation: That is the fuse's mechanism.
Breakers do not rely on heating.
The electromagnet pulls the switch open above the set current.
No timing mechanism is involved.

questions.stem: Compared with a fuse, a circuit breaker:

options.text: works faster and can be reset
options.explanation: Those are the two advantages named for breakers.

options.text: blows once and must be replaced
options.explanation: That describes a fuse.
It carries the full household current until it trips.
Placement is irrelevant to its operation.

questions.stem: The thin wire inside a fuse is held in:

options.explanation: No magnet is inside a fuse.
The fuse is a glass cylinder containing the thin wire.
That is not the fuse's construction.
No iron ring is involved.

questions.stem: Household 'fuse boxes' actually contain:

options.explanation: Modern consumer units hold breakers.
The name is misleading.
Earth rods are outside, not in the box.
The misleadingly named 'fuse box' holds resettable breakers.

questions.stem: A breaker resets after tripping because:

options.explanation: Resetting is a switch action, not a wind-up.
Since no part melts, the switch simply closes again.
Reversal is not part of resetting.
That describes nothing real in a breaker.

questions.stem: State the advantage a circuit breaker has over a fuse.
questions.modelAnswer: It does not melt, so it can be reset and reused, and it trips much faster.

questions.stem: What must both fuses and circuit breakers respond to?
questions.modelAnswer: A current larger than the safe value — the result of a fault or a surge.

questions.stem: Explain why circuit breakers are fitted to the whole house rather than fuses.
questions.modelAnswer: They react faster to overloads and reset once the fault is cleared, so homes recover quickly and stay protected; fuses would need replacing after every single fault.

questions.stem: A surge exceeds a breaker's set current. Describe what happens and why the lights can be restored quickly afterwards.
questions.modelAnswer: The electromagnet switch trips and breaks the circuit at once; because nothing inside melted, resetting the breaker restores the supply immediately.
